items.how_it_compares: Unlike traditional ISP-level blocking, this approach targets global public resolvers, which typically operate independently of local telecommunications regulations.
items.practical_takeaway: Organizations should monitor regional DNS regulations as they may impact the reliability and reachability of services for users in specific jurisdictions.

Then I needed to manage AI agents that run on my laptop, a VM on my laptop, and multiple VMs on my home server. Claude Code has a messaging feature which is very useful, but agents can't see each other when they run on different machines. The Claude in Chrome extension only works for agents running on the same machine, so my remote agents couldn't help me with anything in the browser. It's really handy when they can access services that I'm already signed into. I set out to solve all of these problems and I ended up building Fleetlayer. items.normalized_title: show hn simdrop running ios simulators in the macos finder sidebar
items.raw_summary: Hi HN, I made a small macOS utility for my own iOS simulator workflow. I kept running into two annoyances: getting config files in and out of a simulator is clunky (digging into CoreSimulator UUID folders or running simctl), and on the iPhone Duo simulator I couldn't even drag and drop images onto the window at all. SimDrop puts every running iOS simulator in Finder's sidebar (under Locations) with two folders: - Downloads/ (Files app > On My iPhone > Downloads) - Photos and Videos/ (the simulator's Photos library) Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down. Everything is also reachable from the terminal under ~/Library/CloudStorage/SimDrop-SimDrop/. A couple of caveats up front: - Dragging moves files by default (same as iCloud Drive, because it uses File Provider on the startup volume)—hold Option to copy. - macOS 15+ and iOS simulators only (not physical devices). It's free, open source (GPL-3.0), signed and notarized, and installable via Homebrew: brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop Just sharing in case others run into the same friction—feedback or PRs welcome!

The paper AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design (Mila, McGill, Princeton, UPenn and Erised Labs authors, listed Nov 24, 2026) has four coding agents write hardware code for quantized decoders, in 9,136 attempts. The authors report that feedback pointing to the first state mismatch raised acceptance in all 12 agent and task cells by 25 to 47 points and halved agent-hours per accepted design, and that 45 of 69 accepted designs failed within the 32 steps their tests required when regraded on new sequences. This explainer walks through the numbers and caveats. Honesty line: we read the paper and did not run any of it ourselves. All numbers are the authors' own. Of course at the time I did the vimtutor, but it was too dense for me to remember much from it.
